crepes-dulce-de-leche.title: Dulce de leche crêpes
crepes-dulce-de-leche.intro: Serves 8. Thin crêpes filled with dulce de leche, in a Franco-Argentine spirit. Count 1 to 2 crêpes per person depending on pan size, for 8 to 10 crêpes in total.
steps: Crêpe batter: mix 500 g flour, 8 eggs, 1 litre milk, 100 g melted and cooled butter, 80 g sugar and 1 pinch of salt. Whisk until smooth and fluid, with no lumps.
Rest: cover and chill for at least 30 minutes, ideally 1 hour, so the flour hydrates well.
Cooking: lightly butter a hot non-stick pan. Pour in one ladle of batter, tilt the pan to cover the surface, and cook 1 to 2 minutes per side until golden. Repeat to make 8 to 10 crêpes.
Filling: spread 45 to 60 g dulce de leche on each crêpe while still warm (450 to 500 g total for 8 people). Fold into a triangle, roll, or fold like a wallet.
Finish: serve at once, or reheat for 2 minutes in a 150 °C oven if made ahead. You can add a little lightly sweetened whipped cream or orange zest.
Serve: plate 1 to 2 crêpes per person, with an extra drizzle of dulce de leche if you like.
chemistry: Resting the batter hydrates the starch and relaxes the gluten: the crêpes are more supple and less elastic when cooked.
Dulce de leche concentrates lactose and caramelised sugars: it binds and coats the crêpe without further cooking, especially if the crêpe is still warm.
The golden colour of the crêpe comes from the [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard) between egg proteins and the sugars in milk and sugar.

tarte-citron-menton.title: Menton lemon tart
tarte-citron-menton.intro: French Riviera. Serves 4. Prep: 15 min. Cooking: 1 hour. Rest: 1 hour. A delicate, elegant lemon tart made with sweet pastry and a Menton lemon filling.
steps: For the sweet pastry: mix 250 g flour, 100 g icing sugar, 1 pinch of salt, the zest of 1 untreated lemon, and 125 g cold butter cut into cubes. Rub to a sandy texture, add 1 egg, form a ball, and chill for 1 hour.
Preheat the oven to 170 °C. Roll out the pastry, line a tart tin, prick the base, and blind-bake for 15 minutes.
For the lemon cream: whisk 3 whole eggs with 150 g sugar without making them frothy. Add 12 cl Menton lemon juice and the finely grated zest of 1 untreated lemon. Mix well.
Pour the lemon filling into the pre-baked tart shell.
Lower the oven to 140 °C and bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until the filling is set but still slightly wobbly in the centre.
Let cool completely, then chill before serving.
chemistry: In sweet pastry, the butter coats part of the flour, which limits gluten development and gives a tender, crumbly texture.
In the lemon filling, the eggs set gently during baking; the acidity of Menton lemon helps create a smooth, delicate texture without making the filling heavy.

baba-au-rhum-saint-james.title: Rum baba (Saint James rum)
baba-au-rhum-saint-james.intro: A French classic: small, open-crumbed brioche cakes soaked in a sugar syrup scented with Saint James rum (Martinique). Makes about 6 individual babas. Add the rum once the syrup is warm, never boiling, so you keep its aroma.
steps: Dough: dissolve 20 g fresh baker's yeast in 2–3 tbsp warm milk. In a bowl, mix 250 g flour, 40 g sugar and a pinch of salt; make a well, add 3 whole eggs and the yeast mixture. Knead until smooth and elastic (stand mixer or by hand), then work in 100 g softened butter in several additions until fully absorbed — the same gesture as [bassinage](bassinage), another material.

Cover and rise for about 1 hour at room temperature until doubled. Butter 6 baba moulds (or one large tin), fill about three-quarters full, prove another 30–45 minutes until the dough almost reaches the rim.
Bake at 180 °C for about 20–25 minutes (less for very small moulds) until golden. Unmould while still warm onto a rack.

Syrup: bring 400 ml water, 200 g sugar and 1 split vanilla pod (or a little extract) to the boil; simmer 3–4 minutes then take off the heat. Cool to about 50 °C, then stir in 12–15 cl Saint James rum (adjust to taste).
Soaking: place the babas in a deep dish; soak generously with warm syrup, turn gently so they absorb evenly; repeat if needed after a few minutes. Chill at least 2 hours.
To serve: drain briefly if very wet on top; add a little cold syrup and, if you like, lightly sweetened whipped cream.
chemistry: Yeast ferments sugars into CO₂ and flavour compounds: the bubbles and fermentation alcohol expand the crumb before baking.
Baking sets the egg proteins and gelatinises the flour starch, giving a structure that can hold syrup without collapsing completely. The golden crust: [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard).
Sugar in the syrup raises osmotic pressure and helps the baba retain moisture; rum's volatile aromas bind better if the syrup is no longer boiling.

tiramisu.title: Tiramisu
tiramisu.intro: Serves 4. A classic no-bake dessert from Veneto: ladyfinger biscuits (savoiardi) dipped in cold moka-pot coffee, layered with a silky mascarpone cream of eggs and sugar. Make ahead: chill at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Dust with unsweetened cocoa just before serving.
steps: Coffee: brew 15 cl strong moka-pot coffee, sweeten with 1/2 teaspoon sugar, then cool completely. Add 1 tablespoon Marsala or amber rum if you like.

Yolks: separate 3 very fresh eggs. [Blanchir the yolks](blanchir-les-jaunes): whisk the 3 yolks with 30 g sugar (2 tablespoons) until pale, mousse-like and thick — keep whisking until the mixture holds.
Mascarpone: mix 250 g mascarpone into the yolks until the cream is smooth.
Whites: beat the 3 egg whites, adding 30 g sugar (2 tablespoons) gradually. Whisk until stiff: to check, turn the bowl upside down — the whites should not move.
Cream: fold the whites gently into the mascarpone cream in three additions, without overworking.

Assembly: in a rectangular dish or individual glasses, dip 125 g ladyfinger biscuits (savoiardi, about 12) very briefly in the cold coffee — about one second per side, without soaking them through. Alternate layers of biscuits and cream; finish with a layer of cream.
Rest: cover in contact and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, so the cream sets and the biscuits absorb evenly.
To serve: dust generously with unsweetened bitter cocoa at the last moment.
chemistry: Mascarpone, rich in fat, combines with egg yolks and sugar into a thick, creamy base; folded egg whites add lightness without baking.
Sugar added gradually to the whites holds water in the foam, so the meringue stays stiff enough to hold if you turn the bowl upside down.
A very quick dip limits water uptake: the biscuits stay soft inside while taking on the coffee aroma.
Chilling stabilises the cream and lets coffee and Marsala flavours spread evenly; bitter cocoa balances the sweetness of sugar and mascarpone.

fondant-chocolat.title: Chocolate fondant
fondant-chocolat.intro: Serves 4. A small dark-chocolate cake baked in a very hot oven: the edges set, the centre stays molten. Make the batter ahead; it can wait in the fridge. Bake at the last moment.
steps: Tins: butter 4 ramekins and dust with unsweetened cocoa or a little flour, then tap out the excess.
Chocolate: melt 120 g dark chocolate (70%) with 120 g unsalted butter over a bain-marie until smooth. Let it cool slightly.
Batter: whisk 3 eggs with 60 g sugar (3 tablespoons) just enough to combine, without adding much air. Pour in the warm chocolate, then mix in 40 g flour and a pinch of salt until smooth.
Fill: divide the batter among the ramekins. They can wait in the fridge for up to 24 hours.
Baking: oven preheated to 200 °C. Bake 8 to 10 minutes: the edges should be set and the centre still wobbly. Overbake and the heart sets.
To serve: rest 1 to 2 minutes, then unmould or serve in the ramekin. Serve at once.
chemistry: Cocoa butter melts at a low temperature: in the centre of the cake it stays liquid and gives the molten core.
At the edges, egg proteins coagulate and flour starch gelatinises: that is what forms the shell.
A very hot oven and a short bake cook the outside before the centre reaches setting temperature.

oeufs-a-la-neige.title: Œufs à la neige
oeufs-a-la-neige.intro: Serves 4. A French classic, also called floating islands: poached mounds of whipped whites on a crème anglaise. A thread of caramel. The poaching milk becomes the custard. Make the cream ahead, chilled; poach the snows at the last moment, or keep them warm.
steps: Whites: separate 4 very fresh eggs. Whip the 4 whites with a pinch of salt. Add 40 g sugar (2 tablespoons) gradually. Beat until very firm: to check, turn the bowl upside down — the whites must not move.
Milk: flatten a vanilla pod, split it, scrape the seeds. Heat 50 cl milk with the seeds and the pod to 80–85 °C, covered. The milk shivers; it does not boil.

Poach: shape quenelles with two spoons, slip them into the milk. 2 minutes on one side, turn, 2 minutes on the other. They swell. Drain on a cloth. The milk stays — it is the base of the crème anglaise.

Crème anglaise: [blanchir the yolks](blanchir-les-jaunes) — whisk the 4 yolks with 60 g sugar (3 tablespoons), without adding much air. Pour in the hot milk gradually. Return to a low heat to 82–84 °C, coating the back of the spoon. Do not boil — overcook and it splits. Strain. Cool.
Caramel: as for the [crème caramel](creme-caramel) — pour 2 tablespoons water (30 g) over 80 g sugar. Do not stir. Blond amber.
To serve: a pool of cold crème anglaise, the snows on top, a thread of caramel. Toasted flaked almonds, if you like.
chemistry: The proteins of the whites (ovalbumin) denature under the whisk and trap air. Sugar holds the water: a firm snow.
At 80–85 °C the surface proteins set: the foam holds without collapsing. At a boil the bubbles burst.
The yolks, at 82–84 °C, bind the milk: lecithin, gentle coagulation. Past 85 °C it splits.
The caramel, as for the crème caramel: sugar pushed without stirring. One crystal restarts the whole recrystallisation.

figures.caption: Firm whites: a pinch of salt, 40 g sugar added gradually. Bowl upside down, they do not move.
Quenelles in milk at 80–85 °C. 2 minutes each side. The milk does not boil; it will make the crème anglaise.
Yolks and milk to 82–84 °C: coating the back of the spoon. Past that, it splits.
Cold crème anglaise, the snows on top, a thread of blond caramel. As for the crème caramel: do not stir the sugar.

pot-au-feu.title: Pot-au-feu
pot-au-feu.intro: Serves 6 to 8. Classic French bourgeois dish: beef cuts (shank, chuck, brisket) and marrow bones simmered slowly with carrots, leeks, turnips, celery and onions in a broth flavoured with bouquet garni. Slow cooking for 3 to 4 hours to achieve tender meat and rich broth. Traditionally served with vegetables and bread, but also pairs beautifully with gnocchi for a modern variation.
steps: Meats and bones: count about 1.2 to 1.5 kg of meat in total for 6 to 8 people. Choose 400 to 500 g beef shank, 400 to 500 g chuck or blade, 300 to 400 g brisket with bone, and 3 to 4 marrow bones. Rinse the meats in cold water and pat dry.

Cold water start: in a large pot, place all the meats and bones. Cover generously with cold water (about 3 to 4 litres), add 1 teaspoon of coarse salt. Bring very slowly to a boil uncovered: this gradual rise allows proteins to coagulate on the surface.
Skimming: as soon as the first tremors appear, carefully skim off the grey foam rising to the surface. Repeat several times during the first 20 minutes to obtain a clear broth.

Aromatics and vegetables: after the initial skimming, add 2 onions each studded with 2 cloves, 1 bouquet garni (thyme, bay, parsley), 2 garlic cloves in their skin. Simmer at very low boil for 2 hours.

Adding garnish vegetables: after 2 hours, add 4 to 5 carrots peeled and cut into chunks, 3 to 4 leeks washed and tied, 2 to 3 turnips peeled and cut into quarters, 2 celery stalks. Continue cooking 1½ to 2 more hours, until the meats are very tender and fall apart with a fork.
Marrow bones: remove the marrow bones after 1½ hours total cooking time to prevent them from emptying completely; keep warm in a little broth.
Degreasing: at the end of cooking, carefully remove the meats and vegetables. Degrease the broth on the surface with a ladle or paper towel.

Traditional plating: slice the meats, arrange in a serving dish with vegetables around. Drizzle with a little broth. Serve the marrow bones separately, with coarse salt and toasted bread. Accompany with gherkins, Dijon mustard and fleur de sel.

Gnocchi variation: for a modern presentation, serve the pot-au-feu with Italian-style gnocchi cooked in salted boiling water, drained and tossed in butter. Arrange the gnocchi on the plate, place a few slices of meat and vegetables, drizzle generously with hot broth.
chemistry: Starting with cold water allows gradual extraction of soluble proteins and collagen; the slow temperature rise favours their coagulation on the surface rather than in the broth, which facilitates skimming and gives a clear consommé.
Long cooking at low boil (92 to 95 °C) transforms collagen from gelatinous meats (shank, chuck, brisket) into gelatin: fibres relax, meat becomes tender and the broth gains body and richness.
Marrow bones release their lipids and gelatin into the broth; removed after 1½ hours, they keep their creamy marrow for serving, while the broth has already captured their aromas.

Vegetables added mid-cooking bring sugars, aromas and body to the broth without completely breaking down; their volatile compounds (carrots, celery, leeks) enrich the aromatic palette of the consommé.
The onion studded with cloves and the bouquet garni structure the aromatic background: eugenol from cloves, thymol from thyme and lactones from bay leaf diffuse slowly during hours of simmering.
Degreasing at the end of cooking removes excess surface lipids while preserving dissolved gelatin and umami compounds, for a broth that is both powerful and light on the palate.

poire-belle-helene.title: Poire Belle Hélène
poire-belle-helene.intro: Serves 4. Paris, 1864. Jacques Offenbach opens La Belle Hélène at the Variétés: Helen of Sparta as opéra-bouffe, the Second Empire laughing at Homer. Auguste Escoffier gives a dessert the same name: a Williams pear poached in vanilla, vanilla ice cream, a hot chocolate sauce, almonds. Hot over cold. Poach the pears ahead; make the sauce at the last moment.
steps: The name: on 17 December 1864, at the Théâtre des Variétés, La Belle Hélène fills the house. This is not Homer's Helen — it is the Paris farce. Escoffier, still young, gives the dessert the title of the operetta. The pear, the ice cream, the scalding chocolate: three temperatures, one gesture.
Pears: 4 firm Williams, not too ripe. Peel, keeping the stem. Core from the base. Rub with lemon at once — without acid they brown.
Syrup: 1 litre water, 200 g sugar, 1 split vanilla pod, the juice of half a lemon. Bring to a simmer.
Poach: lower the pears in. 20 to 25 minutes, a blade goes in, they still hold. Cool in the syrup — they take the vanilla.
Chocolate sauce: melt 120 g dark chocolate (70%) with 12 cl crème fleurette and 1 spoon of the syrup, over a bain-marie. Keep hot: it must reach the table scalding.
To serve: a drained pear, a scoop of vanilla ice cream beside it. Spoon the chocolate in front of the guest. Toasted flaked almonds.
chemistry: Lemon holds back polyphenol oxidase: without acid the flesh browns in air.
In the syrup, heat loosens the pectin; sugar enters by osmosis. Williams, with fine flesh, poaches without collapsing.
Chocolate and cream: a cocoa-butter emulsion. Served hot it stays fluid; on the ice it begins to set. That is Escoffier's contrast.

figures.caption: Peel, keeping the stem. Core from the base. Lemon: without acid the flesh browns.
Vanilla syrup, a simmer. 20 to 25 minutes. Cool in the syrup: the pear takes the vanilla.
Chocolate and cream over a bain-marie. Scalding at the table, over the ice: hot over cold.

cavatelli-pesto.title: Cavatelli with pesto
cavatelli-pesto.intro: Serves 4. Puglian-style cavatelli made with only 2 ingredients: semola di grano duro rimacinata and water. They are served with a Ligurian-style pesto made from fresh basil from Frejus, pine nuts, Carapelli olive oil, Parmigiano Reggiano, and garlic.
steps: Dough: count 100 g semola di grano duro rimacinata per person. For 4 people, mix 400 g semola with lukewarm water little by little until you have a firm, smooth, workable dough — that is [bassinage](bassinage). Knead for a few minutes, then rest it covered for 20 to 30 minutes — that is [détente](detente).
Shaping: roll the dough into ropes, cut small pieces, then drag them with your fingers or a butter knife to form the cavatelli. Lay them on a lightly floured cloth or tray.
Pesto: blend or pound fresh basil from Frejus with 1 to 2 garlic cloves, pine nuts, grated Parmigiano Reggiano, and Carapelli olive oil until smooth and fragrant. Season lightly if needed.
Cooking: boil the cavatelli in a large pan of salted water until they rise to the surface and are tender but still slightly firm.
Finish: loosen the pesto with a little pasta cooking water, coat the cavatelli gently off the heat, and serve at once with a little extra Parmigiano Reggiano if you like.
chemistry: Semola di grano duro rimacinata absorbs water gradually and creates an elastic dough that keeps its shape well in boiling water, even without egg.
A little pasta water helps bind the oil, cheese, and water in the pesto around the pasta, making the sauce smoother and more even.

gnocchi-daube.title: Gnocchi à la daube
gnocchi-daube.intro: Serves 4. A Nice classic: potato gnocchi napped with a beef daube — meat simmered in red wine, [passata](passata), orange and herbs. In Nice, the daube does not only meet pasta: it finds the gnocchi. Make the daube ahead; the gnocchi at the last moment.
steps: Daube — meat: 1 kg chuck or beef cheek, in large cubes. In a cocotte, hot [olive oil](huile): brown the meat on all sides, then reserve.

Daube — base: in the same pot, sweat 2 onions and 2 carrots in [brunoise](brunoise), 3 garlic cloves. Return the meat. Deglaze with 500 ml Provençal red wine. Add 400 g [passata](passata), 1 untreated orange zest, thyme, bay, 2 cloves, salt, pepper.

Simmer: cover lightly. Mijoter 2½ to 3 hours over very low heat until the meat falls apart (see [Mijoter](mijoter)). If the sauce reduces too far, a little water. Remove zest, bay and cloves. Adjust seasoning — the sauce should nap.

Gnocchi: 800 g floury potatoes (Bintje), cooked in their skins. Peel while still hot, pass through a ricer. On the board, 200 to 250 g flour, 1 egg, a pinch of salt. Knead just enough. Ropes, pieces, fork ridges.
Cooking and service: boiling salted water. Once the gnocchi rise, 30 seconds more. Drain, nap with hot daube. A little flat-leaf parsley. No cheese — or a little Parmigiano, according to the table.
chemistry: At low temperature, collagen in the chuck turns to gelatin: the meat melts, the sauce thickens without flour.
Wine and passata acidify; orange zest, a Niçois touch, lifts without sweetening.
Floury potatoes take little flour: light gnocchi that carry the daube without hardening.

gnocchi-parisienne.title: Gnocchi à la parisienne
gnocchi-parisienne.intro: Serves 6. Gnocchi à la parisienne after Escoffier: a milk choux paste enriched with potato purée, eggs, Gruyère and nutmeg. Poach, then gratinate under [Mornay sauce](sauce-mornay). These are not the Niçois [gnocchi à la daube](gnocchi-daube), nor gnocchi alla romana with semolina.
steps: Choux paste: in a pan, 500 ml [milk](lait), 100 g [butter](beurre), a pinch of salt, a touch of pepper. Bring to a boil. Off the heat, tip in 250 g flour all at once; stir hard until absorbed. Return over low heat to dry out — the paste pulls from the pan and the spatula.

Purée: 600 g floury potatoes, cooked in their skins, peeled while still hot. Pass through a ricer or food mill — never mash by crushing: tap, do not make glue. Fold the purée at once into the still-hot choux paste.
Eggs and cheese: let cool slightly. Beat in 6 whole eggs, one by one, until a smooth paste that forms a beak. Add 150 g grated Gruyère and a good grating of nutmeg — essential.
Poach: simmering water, lightly salted — not a hard boil. Piping bag, or two wet spoons if one has no bag. Small nuggets about 3 cm. Once they rise and swell, about 3 minutes; drain.

Gratin: butter a dish. A little [Mornay sauce](sauce-mornay) on the bottom — quite napping, loosened a little if it has thickened. Arrange the gnocchi in two or three layers, nap with the rest (about ¾ litre for 6). Sprinkle with Gruyère. Fairly hot oven, until golden.
Without a bag: flour the board, form small quenelles with a wet spoon, poach the same way. One can also fry a few, larger, in a basket — another presentation, same batter.
chemistry: Choux paste traps steam: it swells when poached; in the oven under Mornay, it puffs a little more.
Floury purée lightens and stretches the batter; too much water in the potato, or a blender, and the paste sticks, the gnocchi turn heavy.
Nutmeg and Gruyère season; [Mornay](sauce-mornay) protects from drying and browns without drowning — too thin, they will not hold.

ravioli-pesto-di-liguria.title: Ravioli pesto di Liguria
ravioli-pesto-di-liguria.intro: Serves 4. Ravioli made with semola di grano duro rimacinata and whole eggs, filled with ricotta and spinach, and served with a Ligurian-style pesto of basil, pine nuts, Parmigiano Reggiano, olive oil, garlic and a touch of lemon.
steps: Dough: count 100 g semola di grano duro rimacinata and 1 whole egg per person. For 4 people, mix 400 g semola with 4 eggs until you have a homogeneous dough, adding a little warm water if needed. Wrap in cling film and rest for 30 minutes in the fridge — that is [détente](detente).

Filling: mix 250 g ricotta for 4 people, which is about 62.5 g per person, with 300 g fresh spinach reduced in olive oil, the Italian way, not in water, then well drained and chopped. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg so the filling stays neat and not too wet.
Pesto: count half a basil plant and half a garlic clove per person, plus pine nuts, Parmigiano Reggiano, olive oil and a pinch of lemon. Blend or pound until smooth and fragrant.
Assembly: roll the dough thinly, add small portions of filling, close and shape the ravioli, pressing out the air around the filling.

Cooking and finish: cook the ravioli in a large pan of boiling salted water until cooked through but still delicate. Lift them out of the water, then finish them gently in butter with a few sage leaves, just for the aroma. Remove the sage when plating, then finish with the pesto.
chemistry: Semola di grano duro rimacinata and whole eggs make a supple but sturdy dough, well suited to a moist filling like ricotta and spinach.
Squeezing the spinach well limits free water in the filling, which helps the ravioli seal properly and makes them less likely to burst during cooking.
Lemon lifts the pesto without making it sour: a small amount is enough to freshen the basil and balance the richness of the cheese and olive oil.

cannelloni-ricotta-epinards.title: Ricotta & spinach cannelloni
cannelloni-ricotta-epinards.intro: Serves 4. Cannelloni whose “pasta” is a savoury crêpe, filled with ricotta and spinach, napped with [béchamel](sauce-bechamel) and a little [tomato sauce](passata), then gratinated.
steps: Crêpes: mix 250 g flour, 4 eggs, 50 cl milk, 40 g melted cooled butter and a pinch of salt — no sugar. Whisk until smooth, rest 30 minutes. Butter a hot pan and cook 8 thin crêpes, 1 to 2 minutes per side.
Filling: mix 250 g ricotta with 300 g fresh spinach reduced in olive oil, the Italian way, not in water, then well drained and chopped. Salt, pepper and nutmeg, so the filling stays neat.
Assembly: spread the filling on each crêpe and roll it tightly into a cylinder, like a cannellone. Seam underneath.
Dish: butter a gratin dish. Spoon a little [tomato sauce](passata) on the base. Arrange the cannelloni, nap with [béchamel](sauce-bechamel), a little more tomato, and grated Parmigiano Reggiano.
Baking: oven at 180 °C for 20 to 25 minutes, until the gratin is golden. Serve hot.
chemistry: The crêpe is already cooked: the oven only heats the filling and gratinates the sauces, without hardening raw pasta.
Squeezing the spinach well keeps water out of the dish; otherwise the béchamel thins and the crêpes go soggy.
Béchamel keeps the crêpes from drying; the acidity of the tomato balances the richness of the ricotta.

linguine-ai-frutti-di-mare.title: Linguine ai frutti di mare
linguine-ai-frutti-di-mare.intro: Serves 4. Bronze-cut linguine, 2 scallops and 3 prawns per person, baby octopus (poulpettes). Sauce: [passata](passata) built on a prawn bisque. No Parmigiano — finish with pan grattato. Oval platter — copper or stainless — cooking and serving.
steps: Seafood: 8 scallops (2 per person), 12 prawns (3 per person), 300 g baby octopus (poulpettes). Peel the prawns keeping heads and shells for the bisque — as for [Crevettes Provençales](gambas-provencales-pastis); remove the vein. Pat the scallops dry. Rinse and dry the poulpettes.

Bisque: in a pan, [olive oil](huile), heads and shells 3 to 4 minutes over medium heat. 1 shallot, 1 garlic clove. Cover with 400 ml water. Simmer 15 to 20 minutes. Strain, pressing well — an iodised, napping jus.
Pan grattato: 60 g dried breadcrumbs. Dry pan or with 1 tablespoon olive oil, medium heat, until golden and crisp. Reserve — no Parmigiano.

Searing: 35 cm oval platter, copper or stainless, or a sauté pan. Very hot olive oil, 2 sliced garlic cloves, 30 seconds. Scallops 1 minute per side, prawns 1 minute per side, poulpettes 2 to 3 minutes. Reserve.

Passata-bisque sauce: in the same dish, 300 g [passata](passata), then the strained bisque. A trickle of oil, salt, pepper, a pinch of Espelette if wished. 4 to 5 minutes over medium heat, until napping — the passata takes on the taste of the sea.
Linguine: 400 g bronze-cut linguine. Boiling salted water, al dente minus 1 minute.

Finish: linguine in the dish, a little cooking water, the sauce. Toss 1 minute. Return scallops, prawns, poulpettes. Flat-leaf parsley. Scatter pan grattato generously. Carry the oval platter to the table at once.
chemistry: Heads and shells release iodine and umami into the bisque; [passata](passata) thickens and acidifies it without cream.
Toasted pan grattato brings crunch and Maillard — the role of Parmigiano on a seafood pasta, without milk.
Scallops, prawns and poulpettes turn rubbery if left too long: short sear, then only reheat in the sauce.
The rough bronze-cut pasta surface catches sauce and crumbs.

figures.caption: Bisque: prawn heads and shells roasted in [olive oil](huile), then strained.
Pan grattato: dried breadcrumbs toasted in the pan — no Parmigiano.
Passata-bisque sauce: [passata](passata) built on the strained bisque, until napping.
Oval platter — copper or stainless. Linguine, seafood, pan grattato.

risotto-osso-buco.title: Risotto with osso buco
risotto-osso-buco.intro: Serves 4. A Milan-inspired creamy risotto served with slowly braised veal osso buco, its reduced cooking juices and, if you like, a little gremolata to finish.
steps: Osso buco: brown 4 slices of veal shank in a little olive oil, then set aside. In the same pot, sweat onion, carrot and celery. Add a little tomato paste if you like, return the meat, deglaze with white wine, then add light stock. Add thyme or bay and simmer gently until the meat is very tender.

Prepare the juices and garnish: once the veal is tender, remove the slices and strain or reduce the cooking juices slightly to concentrate them. Shred the meat or keep the pieces whole depending on how you want to plate it.

Risotto: sweat 1 shallot in butter or olive oil, add 400 g carnaroli rice and toast it for 1 to 2 minutes. Add hot stock gradually, stirring regularly, until the rice is creamy but still slightly al dente.
Finish the risotto: off the heat, stir in cold butter and grated Parmigiano Reggiano for a supple, glossy texture. Adjust with a little cooking juice if needed.

To plate: serve the risotto in the plate, add the osso buco on top or alongside, then spoon over a little reduced jus. Finish, if you like, with gremolata made with lemon zest, garlic and parsley for freshness and lift.
chemistry: Long cooking gradually turns the shank's collagen into gelatin, which gives the osso buco its tender texture and the juices more body.
Carnaroli rice releases its starch gradually as it cooks, which is what gives risotto its natural creamy bind without needing cream.
Butter and cheese added off the heat form an emulsion with the rice starch and remaining liquid, making the risotto more silky and glossy.

risotto-gambas.title: Prawn risotto (risotto alle gamberi)
risotto-gambas.intro: Serves 4. A carnaroli risotto with natural saffron, scented with a rosé-wine prawn stock, then topped with peeled prawns quickly seared. Peeling the prawns is an essential step: it yields an iodine-rich stock and allows the flesh to cook without the shell.
steps: Peel the prawns: count 2 raw prawns per person (8 for 4 people). Twist off the head gently; reserve heads and shells for the stock. Remove the shell by sliding your thumb under the legs and pulling towards the tail; keep or remove the tail depending on how you want to plate. Make a shallow cut along the back with the tip of a knife and remove the dark intestinal vein. Rinse the bodies briefly and pat dry.

Prawn stock: in a saucepan, sauté the heads and shells with a drizzle of olive oil for 2 to 3 minutes, deglaze with rosé wine (no water) and a little salt, simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, then strain carefully. Keep the stock very hot.

Risotto: in a sauté pan, heat a drizzle of olive oil, add 400 g carnaroli rice and toast for 1 to 2 minutes, stirring. Deglaze with 10 cl dry white wine, then add the prawn stock gradually, stirring regularly. After 5 minutes of cooking, add a pinch of natural saffron filaments directly to the pan (never powdered saffron). Continue cooking for about 18 to 20 minutes in total, until the rice is creamy but still slightly al dente.
Prawns: in a separate pan with a drizzle of olive oil, sear the peeled prawns for 1 to 2 minutes on each side until just cooked and lightly pink. Season with salt and pepper.
Finish the risotto: off the heat, finish with 80 g cold French butter in pieces and 80 g grated Parmigiano Reggiano for a supple, glossy texture. Adjust salt and pepper.
Plating: spoon the risotto into the bowl or plate and arrange the prawns on top.
chemistry: Heads and shells release iodine-rich, umami compounds into the stock, which slowly seasons the rice during cooking.
Carnaroli rice releases starch gradually; finishing off the heat with French butter and Parmigiano Reggiano forms the classic creamy risotto emulsion.
Natural saffron filaments, added directly to the sauté pan after 5 minutes of cooking, hydrate in the stock and release finer colour and aroma than industrial powder.
Peeling and drying the prawns before a quick sear limits excess moisture and helps avoid rubbery flesh.

risotto-safran-fruits-de-mer.title: Saffron risotto & seafood
risotto-safran-fruits-de-mer.intro: Serves 4. Carnaroli risotto with saffron, moistened with homemade stock. On top: prawns — heads off, tails on — poulpitos fried with cherry tomatoes and red wine, and scallops just seared.
steps: Prawns: 8 raw prawns. Twist off the head. Peel the body, keep the tail. Score the back, pull the vein. Pat dry.

Poulpitos: 400 g baby octopus, rinsed, well dried. Very hot pan, a drizzle of [olive oil](huile). Fry until golden. Add 250 g cherry tomatoes, then 10 cl red wine. Reduce 3 to 4 minutes, until the skins wrinkle and the juices coat. Reserve with the jus.

Risotto: sweat 1 [sliced shallot](emincer) in the oil. Add 400 g carnaroli rice, toast 1 to 2 minutes. Then 10 cl white wine, 90 seconds, until absorbed. Add homemade stock, kept hot, gradually, stirring. After 5 minutes, a pinch of saffron threads. 18 to 20 minutes in all, creamy, still a little al dente.
Scallops: 8 noix, well dried. Very hot pan, a drizzle of oil. 1 minute per side, just set. See the [scallop ravioli](ravioli-saint-jacques).
Prawns: in a hot pan, a drizzle of oil, 1 minute per side, until pink. Salt.
Finish: off the heat, mount the risotto with 80 g cold French butter in pieces and 200 g grated Parmigiano Reggiano. Salt, white pepper.
Plating: the risotto, the prawns tail up, the poulpitos with the cherry tomatoes and a little jus, the scallops. Chopped flat-leaf parsley, if you like.
chemistry: Prawn flesh, overcooked, turns rubbery: one minute is enough. The tail stays for the plate.
The poulpitos, small, are fried: the skin browns — [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard). Then the cherry tomatoes give their juice; the red wine deglazes, acidity against the iodine.
The scallop sets in one minute: longer, it weeps and tightens.
Carnaroli rice releases starch; butter and Parmigiano Reggiano, off the heat, emulsify with that starch. Saffron threads, after 5 minutes, colour and perfume.

figures.caption: Prawns: head off, tail on. Vein removed.
Poulpitos fried, cherry tomatoes, red wine. Reduce until the juices coat.

risotto-aux-truffes.title: Truffle risotto
risotto-aux-truffes.intro: Serves 4. Carnaroli risotto finished with butter and Parmigiano Reggiano, scented with black truffle. The truffle goes in off the heat — grated or shaved — to keep its volatile perfume.
steps: Stock: bring 1.2 litres chicken or vegetable stock to a simmer. Keep it very hot.
Risotto: sweat 1 [sliced shallot](emincer) in 30 g French butter. Add 400 g carnaroli rice, toast 1 to 2 minutes. Deglaze with 10 cl dry white wine, until absorbed.
Cooking: add the hot stock gradually, ladle by ladle, stirring. 18 to 20 minutes in all — creamy, still slightly al dente.
Finish: off the heat, mount with 80 g cold French butter in pieces and 80 g grated Parmigiano Reggiano. Soft, glossy texture. Salt, white pepper.
Truffle: grate or finely shave 20 to 30 g black truffle (fresh, or preserved in its juice). Stir half in off the heat; arrange the rest over the risotto when plating. Serve at once.
chemistry: Carnaroli rice releases starch gradually; butter and Parmigiano Reggiano, off the heat, form the creamy risotto emulsion — without cream.
Truffle aromas are volatile: high heat drives them off. Add the truffle off the heat, or only at the finish.
The fat in butter and cheese carries the truffle's aromatic compounds and holds them on the plate.

tian-provencal.title: Provençal tian
tian-provencal.intro: Serves 4. A Provençal summer dish: rounds of courgette, aubergine, tomato and onion, stood upright in a tian — the earthenware dish that gave the recipe its name — then baked slowly with olive oil, garlic and herbs.
steps: Vegetables: wash 2 courgettes, 2 medium aubergines and 4 firm tomatoes. Peel 2 onions. Cut everything into even rounds about 5 mm thick.
Tian: oil an oval oven dish generously (a tian or gratin dish). Rub the base with 1 cut garlic clove.
Assembly: stand the rounds upright, packed tightly, alternating along the dish: courgette, tomato, aubergine, onion, and so on, until the tian is full.
Seasoning: drizzle 6 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, add 1 sliced garlic clove, fresh thyme or herbes de Provence, salt and pepper. Another trickle of oil over the top.
Baking: 180 °C for 50 to 60 minutes. The edges should brown and the juices concentrate in the base. If the top dries too much, cover with baking paper for the last 20 minutes.
Serving: rest 10 minutes. Serve warm, as a main or beside a [roast](steak-au-poivre-veau), a [tournedos](tournedos-boeuf-tian) or fish.
chemistry: Long dry heat concentrates the sugars in tomatoes and onions; water evaporates and flavour intensifies.
Olive oil conducts heat and stops the vegetables sticking; it also carries the aromas of thyme and garlic.
Packing the rounds tightly limits shrinkage: they stay standing as they cook instead of collapsing.

gambas-provencales-pastis.title: Crevettes Provençales
gambas-provencales-pastis.intro: Serves 4. Four very large gambas — langoustine size — per plate, head and tail on, cooked with garlic, parsley and pastis. Beside them: grenaille potatoes cut in half, well done, 4 minutes per side in the sauté pan, very hot extra-virgin olive oil. Cherry tomatoes with their leaves. Minimal plating.
steps: Grenaille: wash 8 to 12 small grenaille potatoes, cut them in half. Very hot sauté pan, extra-virgin olive oil. Lay the halves cut-side down, 4 minutes per side, until well done and golden. Salt. Set aside.
Gambas: count 4 very large gambas per person, langoustine size (16 for 4). Leave them whole: head and tail. Slit the back, pull out the intestinal vein. Pat dry.
Sear: in the same pan, very hot extra-virgin olive oil. Sear the gambas 1 to 2 minutes per side, until pink. Salt at the end of cooking.
Persillade: slice 2 garlic cloves. Add the garlic and a handful of chopped flat-leaf parsley. 30 seconds, without burning the garlic.

Pastis: measure 8 cl into a glass — never pour from the bottle. Pour into the pan, keep your face back. Light at the rim with a long kitchen lighter, or let it reduce 1 minute. Keep a lid within reach.
Plating: 4 whole gambas per plate, a few grenaille halves, 2 or 3 cherry tomatoes with their leaves. A little pastis jus. Nothing more.
chemistry: Four minutes a side colour the grenaille: [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard), starch cooked through, skin crisp.
Gambas flesh sets in 1 to 2 minutes: longer and it turns rubbery.
Pastis, at about 45%, ignites like cognac: the alcohol burns off, anethole — the same aroma as fennel — stays. Garlic and parsley are the Provençal persillade.
Cherry tomatoes, with their leaves, stay raw: fresh acidity against the oil and the anise.

figures.caption: Grenaille potatoes cut in half. Sauté pan, very hot extra-virgin olive oil, 4 minutes per side, well done.
Persillade: 2 sliced garlic cloves, a handful of flat-leaf parsley.
8 cl pastis, measured into a glass. Flambé at the rim, or reduce 1 minute.

polenta-ragu-entrecote.title: Polenta, ragù d'entrecôte
polenta-ragu-entrecote.intro: Serves 4. Limousin beef entrecôte seared 4 minutes per side, then returned to a ragù: juices deglazed with red wine, shallots, pomodoro [passata](passata), water, salt, pepper and piment d'Espelette. Two hours at a simmer, until the meat falls apart. Polenta cooked in milk and butter. Served with Parmigiano Reggiano.
steps: Entrecôte: take 4 Limousin entrecôtes (200–250 g) out 15–20 min ahead. Very hot pan, extra-virgin olive oil. Sear 4 minutes per side. Lift the meat out and set it aside.
Deglaze: in the same pan, pour 25 cl red wine over the entrecôte juices. Scrape the pan. Reduce by half.
Shallots: émincer 4 shallots (see [Émincer](emincer)). Add them to the reduced wine. Sweat until translucent.
Pomodoro: add 700 g [passata](passata), a little water, salt, pepper and 1 teaspoon piment d'Espelette. Bring to a simmer.
Simmer: return the entrecôte to the ragù. Cover barely. Simmer 2 hours over low heat, until the meat falls apart (see [Simmer](mijoter)). If the sauce reduces too far, a little water.
Polenta: bring 1 litre milk to the boil. Rain in 250 g instant polenta while whisking. It sets in 2 to 3 minutes. Off the heat, beat in 60 g butter. The polenta should stay soft; it spreads.
Plating: spoon the polenta, set the fallen-apart entrecôte on top, nap with the ragù. Grated Parmigiano Reggiano at the table.
chemistry: Four minutes a side colour the meat: [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard), juices on the pan floor.
Red wine deglazes those juices; the alcohol leaves, the acidity stays. The shallots, after, sweeten the base.
Back in the pomodoro, the entrecôte simmers 2 hours: collagen melts, the meat falls apart, the ragù thickens. Water, salt, pepper and piment d'Espelette carry the sauce.
Polenta gelatinises in milk: lactose and milk proteins make a cream; butter, off the heat, emulsifies.

figures.caption: Sear the entrecôte 4 minutes per side, very hot pan. Lift it out.
Deglaze the juices with red wine (25 cl). Scrape the pan, reduce by half.
Then the finely sliced shallots (see [Émincer](emincer)), into the reduced wine.
Passata, water, salt, pepper, piment d'Espelette. Return the entrecôte. Simmer 2 hours, until it falls apart.
Instant polenta in milk: rain 250 g into 1 litre milk, 2 to 3 minutes, then 60 g butter off the heat.

fenouil-caramelise.title: Pan-caramelized fennel
fenouil-caramelise.intro: Serves 4. Preparation 5 minutes, cooking 15 to 20 minutes. A starter of pan-caramelized fennel: quarters seared in sweetened butter, simmered in vegetable stock, then glazed in the reduction.
steps: Fennel: trim 3 to 4 medium bulbs. Cut each into quarters. Remove the outer leaves if they are too tough. Keep the fronds for serving.
Caramel base: in a large frying pan over medium heat, melt 50 g butter with ½ tsp salt and 3 tsp sugar. Add 1 tsp fennel seeds if using.
Searing: place the quarters cut-side down in the pan. Fry for about 30 seconds.
Stock: pour in enough vegetable stock to come about two-thirds of the way up the fennel.

Simmer: cover with a lid, or preferably with a parchment-paper cartouche pierced with a few holes to let steam escape. Simmer gently for about 10 minutes: the fennel should be tender but still slightly firm, only half-cooked.
Reduce: lift the quarters out carefully and set aside. Continue cooking the stock and butter until it reduces to a thick, caramel-like consistency.
Caramelize: return the fennel to the pan, again cut-side down. Fry until the cut faces are deep golden brown.
Serve: transfer to a serving dish and finish with chopped fresh fennel fronds.
chemistry: Sugar and butter form a caramel base: sucrose melts and browns, and the milk solids in the butter add colour.
Fennel is rich in natural sugars and in anethole, the aniseed aroma; the cut face browns faster against the caramel.
Stock to two-thirds of the height steams the vegetable without drowning it; the cartouche lets steam escape so the liquid can reduce.
The reduction concentrates stock and butter into a syrupy glaze that coats the quarters when they go back in the pan.

tournedos-canard-aligot.title: Duck tournedos & aligot
tournedos-canard-aligot.intro: Serves 4. Duck magret cut as tournedos, seared 4 minutes per side, then 10 minutes in the oven at 200 °C. Served on still-hot [aligot](aligot), napped with a redcurrant coulis, deglazed with the juice of 1 lemon.
steps: Aligot: prepare it as for [Aligot](aligot) — Bintje, [tome fraîche](tome-aubrac), food mill, figures of eight until the ribbons. Keep it hot: it sets if it waits.
Tournedos: 2 magrets. Score the skin without cutting into the flesh. Roll each magret, skin out, tightly. Tie. Cut into 3–4 cm tournedos (150–180 g). Take them out 15–20 min ahead.
Sear: very hot sauté pan, extra-virgin olive oil. Sear 4 minutes per side. Lift them out.
Oven: bake the tournedos 10 minutes at 200 °C. Rest 3 to 5 minutes.
Deglaze: in the same pan, pour the juice of 1 lemon over the duck juices. Scrape the pan.
Coulis: in that pan, add 400 g redcurrants. Let them melt 3 to 5 minutes over medium heat, until the coulis coats. Strain if you want a smooth sauce; keep a few whole berries for serving.
Plating: a bed of hot [aligot](aligot). Set the tournedos on top. Nap with the coulis. Serve at once.
chemistry: Four minutes a side colour the duck: [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard), juices on the pan floor.
Ten minutes at 200 °C cook the centre without drying it: the duck fat melts, the flesh stays pink.
Lemon juice deglazes the juices; redcurrants, acid and pectin-rich, bind the coulis without flour: the acidity comes from lemon and redcurrants.
Aligot, with Bintje and [tome](tome-aubrac), stretches in ribbons. It sets if it cools: keep it hot, plate at the last moment.

aligot.title: Aligot
aligot.intro: Serves 4. Aligot from the Aubrac: a purée of floury potatoes — Bintje — worked with [tome fraîche de l'Aubrac](tome-aubrac), butter and [cream](creme), until it makes ribbons. Not Charlotte, not grenaille: too much water, not enough starch, it will not stretch.
steps: Potatoes: 1 kg Bintje, floury. Peel, cut into even pieces. Cold salted water — they grow underground. Bring to a boil, cook about 20 minutes, until a blade goes in. Drain well, let the steam escape 1 minute.
Purée: pass through a food mill, as for the [lamb cutlets](cotelette-agneau-petits-pois-menthe). No blender: it glues the starch.
Garlic: 1 clove, [sliced](emincer), into the still-hot purée.
Butter and cream: 80 g cold [butter](beurre) in pieces, 100 g [crème fraîche](creme). Work in off the heat, salt, white pepper.

Tome: 400 g [tome fraîche de l'Aubrac](tome-aubrac), in thin slices. Return to a very low heat. Add the tome by handfuls, work with a wooden spoon, in figures of eight, until the mass stretches in long ribbons. It pulls away from the pan.
Serve: at once, from the casserole. Aligot that waits sets.
chemistry: Bintje is floury: a lot of dry starch, little water. Firm-fleshed potatoes — Charlotte, grenaille — stay in grains; the aligot will not ribbon.
[Tome fraîche](tome-aubrac), young, melts without oiling off. Its proteins and the Bintje starch form an elastic network: the ribbons.
A blender shears that network: glue, not threads. The mill passes the flesh without beating it.
The figure-of-eight, on a low heat, aligns the proteins. Too hot, the tome splits; too cold, it will not melt.

figures.caption: Bintje, floury. [Tome fraîche de l'Aubrac](tome-aubrac), in slices. Not Charlotte.
Wooden spoon, figures of eight, low heat. The aligot stretches in ribbons.

pommes-boulangere.title: Pommes de terre boulangère
pommes-boulangere.intro: Serves 4. Classic from the baker's oven: potatoes and onions in thin slices, moistened with stock, baked in an oval dish until the top is golden and the bottom melting. No cream — this is not a gratin dauphinois. Serve the dish at the table.
steps: Dish: butter an oval oven dish (as for [gnocchi à la parisienne](gnocchi-parisienne)). Oven at 180 °C.
Cut: peel 1 kg firm potatoes (Charlotte or similar). Slice into even lamelles about 3 mm — [émincer](emincer). Slice 3 yellow onions to the same thickness.
Assembly: alternate layers of potato and onion in the dish, ending with potato. Salt and pepper each layer. Scatter fresh thyme. Dot 40 g [butter](beurre) on top.
Moisten: pour hot chicken or meat stock up to the level of the potatoes — they should bathe, not swim. A trickle of [olive oil](huile) on top.
Cooking: oven 1 h to 1 h 15. The edges should brown, the stock concentrate. If the top burns, cover with parchment for the last 20 minutes. Serve in the oval dish, warm.
chemistry: Potato starch lightly thickens the stock as it cooks: a bound sauce without cream or flour.
Onions melt and sweeten; butter and oil brown the surface by [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard).
Even slices: even cooking. Too thick, the centre stays raw while the top burns.

pommes-safran.title: Potatoes & saffron
pommes-safran.intro: Serves 4. 800 g floury Label Rouge potatoes, pressed through a potato ricer. Six whole garlic cloves, caramelized in olive oil. Then saffron, [butter](beurre) and [cream](creme).
steps: Garlic: peel 6 garlic cloves and leave them whole. Caramelize them gently in 4 tablespoons of olive oil, 8 to 10 minutes, until golden and soft. Set the cloves and the oil aside.

Potatoes: peel 800 g floury Label Rouge potatoes, cut into even pieces and cook in boiling salted water for about 20 minutes, until a knife slips in. Drain well, return to the pan for 1 minute over low heat to drive off the water.
Ricer: press the potatoes while still hot through a potato ricer, fine disc, into a saucepan. Never use a mixer or blender.

Saffron, butter & cream: off the heat, add a pinch of saffron threads to the purée, with 1 tablespoon of the garlic oil, 80 g cold [butter](beurre) in pieces and 80 g [cream](creme). The saffron blends into the purée with the butter and the cream. Salt, and grate a little nutmeg. Lay the 6 whole cloves on the purée. Serve at once.
chemistry: Saffron threads disperse through the hot purée with the butter and the cream: the fat carries the colour and the aroma.
The ricer pushes the flesh through the holes without beating the starch. A mixer shears it and turns the purée gluey.
The oil from the caramelized cloves perfumes the mash without crushing the garlic. Cold butter and cream coat the starch; nutmeg lifts the whole.

comte-morbier-roquefort.title: Comté, Morbier & Roquefort
comte-morbier-roquefort.intro: Cheese is served after the main course, before dessert. At table we offer three AOP cheeses, from mildest to strongest: Comté (Jura, cow's milk, cooked pressed paste), Morbier (Franche-Comté, cow's milk, ash line) and Roquefort (Aveyron, ewe's milk, blue-veined).
steps: Temperature: take the cheeses out of the fridge 30 to 45 minutes before serving. Cold fat is mute: you only taste salt.
Comté: raw cow's milk, cooked pressed paste, aged for months. Firm texture, hazelnut and fruit notes. Cut in thin slices, not cubes.
Morbier: same Jura massif, cow's milk. The black line is vegetable ash: it once protected the evening curd until the morning milk. Softer paste, milky, slightly animal.
Roquefort: ewe's milk, caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon. The blue veins are Penicillium roqueforti. Melting, salty, pungent. A small portion is enough.
Order: Comté first, then Morbier, Roquefort last — the blue would crush anything that follows.
Toursades: this is what we serve with the board, instead of bread. A clean knife between pastes. Wrap each cheese separately for the next day.
chemistry: Comté's ageing breaks down proteins: tyrosine crystals, hazelnut aromas. The older the cheese, the drier and more concentrated the paste.
Morbier's ash is no longer a larder: it remains a visual marker and a slight mineral taste between two curds.
Roquefort is pierced to let air in: Penicillium needs oxygen. Richer ewe's milk carries the blue without making the paste brittle.

tome-aubrac.title: Tome fraîche de l'Aubrac
tome-aubrac.intro: Tome fraîche de l'Aubrac: a young cow's-milk curd from the Aubrac plateau — Aveyron, Cantal, Lozère. Little or no salt. It is the cheese that makes [aligot](aligot) stretch into ribbons.
steps: Nature: white curd, young, elastic. Not an aged tomme. Not Tomme de Savoie. Not Cantal. Not mozzarella.
Cut: in thin slices. It melts into Bintje mash, with butter and [cream](creme).
Aligot: work with a wooden spoon, in figures of eight, on a low heat, until the ribbons. See [Aligot](aligot).
Service: also under [duck tournedos & aligot](tournedos-canard-aligot). Keep it hot: it sets as it cools.
chemistry: Young, its proteins stay intact: elastic. With Bintje starch they form a network — the ribbons of [aligot](aligot).
Too aged, too salty, too pressed: it oils off or breaks. Mozzarella stretches by another network.
If need be: a young Laguiole, or another tome fraîche. Never mozzarella.

vitello-tonnato.title: Vitello tonnato
vitello-tonnato.intro: Serves 6. A dish from Piedmont, served cold: thin slices of veal simmered for 2 hours, topped with tonnato sauce, then finished with a few extra capers. Though it comes from Piedmont, vitello tonnato has become a summer classic on the French Riviera and in Monaco. Make the homemade mayonnaise and tonnato sauce for 6 first (see Homemade mayonnaise and Tonnato sauce). The veal is cooked in a sauté pan and mijoté (see Simmer technique).
steps: Cook the veal in a sauté pan: use about 1 kg veal (topside, eye round or another lean roasting cut). In a wide sauté pan, brown the veal on all sides in a little oil or butter for light colour.

Mijoter for 2 hours: add carrot, onion, celery, bay and a few peppercorns, then add light stock or water to almost cover the veal. Bring to a simmer, cover and mijoter for about 2 hours over very low heat, without a hard boil, until the meat is very tender.
Cooling: let the veal cool in its cooking liquid or wrap it well to keep it moist. Keep this broth for the tonnato sauce.
Tonnato sauce: prepare the tonnato sauce for 6 following the dedicated recipe. You can add a spoonful of the veal cooking liquid for extra harmony with the meat.
Slicing: chill the veal completely, then cut it into very fine, even slices.
Assembly: arrange the veal slices flat on a large platter or individual plates, spoon over a thin layer of tonnato sauce without drowning everything, then add a few capers and some black pepper.
Serving: serve well chilled or at cool room temperature, with a little rocket or a very simple salad if you like, keeping the sauce as the main accent of the dish.
chemistry: Two hours of mijoter turns collagen into gelatin: the veal stays moist and slices finely once chilled.
Chilling firms the meat, which makes thin slicing easier and cleaner, and also helps the tonnato sauce cling better to the surface.
Making the sauce separately lets you adjust seasoning and texture before plating, without touching the veal while it is still warm.

escalope-veau-milanaise-napolitaine.title: Veal milanaise & napolitana
escalope-veau-milanaise-napolitaine.intro: Serves 4. Breaded veal escalope, golden, then [tomato sauce](passata), ham, mozzarella, and under the grill. Milanesa a la napolitana is not from Naples. It is Argentine — Buenos Aires, mid-twentieth century. Italian immigrants brought cotoletta, milanesa alla milanese: breadcrumbs, frying. The topping was born there. The story usually names restaurant Nápoli, on Corrientes: a cook covers a milanesa, puts it under the grill. The name is the restaurant, or the pizza, not the city. In Italy the closer cousin is cotoletta alla bolognese.
steps: Prepare the veal: flatten 4 veal escalopes between two sheets so they are evenly thin. Season lightly with salt and pepper.

Breading: prepare beaten eggs on one side and breadcrumbs mixed with dried parsley and garlic (persillade) on the other. Coat each escalope in breadcrumbs, then egg, then once more in breadcrumbs, pressing lightly so the coating adheres well.
Milanese cooking: pan-fry the escalopes in a butter-and-oil mix or a mild oil until well golden and crisp on both sides. Drain on a rack or paper.

Alla napolitana: place the escalopes on a tray or in a dish. Spoon a little [tomato sauce](passata) or [passata](passata) over each one, add a slice of ham, then sliced or grated mozzarella. A little oregano, if you like.
Finish: put them in the oven or under the grill for a few minutes, just until the mozzarella melts and lightly gratinates. Serve at once, with a simple salad, fries or potatoes if you like.
chemistry: The breadcrumb coating creates a protective layer that browns quickly and helps the escalope stay juicy inside.
The contrast between the crisp crust, tomato sauce, ham and melted mozzarella is what gives the napolitana its identity.
A short finish under the grill melts the cheese without fully soaking the breadcrumb coating.

cotelette-agneau-petits-pois-menthe.title: Lamb cutlets
cotelette-agneau-petits-pois-menthe.intro: Serves 4. Pan-seared lamb cutlets on [potatoes & saffron](pommes-safran), finished with mint cut in julienne, olive oil, lemon, salt and pepper.
steps: Take the cutlets out of the fridge 20 minutes before cooking so they come to room temperature. Season lightly with salt and pepper.
Potatoes & saffron: prepare the [potatoes & saffron](pommes-safran) and keep them warm.
Mint: cut a generous handful of fresh mint leaves into fine julienne. Just before serving, toss with 4 tbsp olive oil, the juice of half a lemon, salt and freshly ground pepper.

Cooking the cutlets: in a very hot pan with a drizzle of olive oil and a little butter, sear 4 lamb cutlets for 3 to 4 minutes on each side for a rosé finish, or a little longer depending on thickness.
Rest: leave the cutlets to rest for 5 minutes under foil before serving.
Plating: spoon the purée in the centre of the plate, place the cutlet on top and scatter the mint julienne over it.
chemistry: Quick cooking over high heat develops [Maillard aromas](reaction-maillard) on the meat while keeping the inside pink and tender.
The [potatoes & saffron](pommes-safran) bring a silky texture and light floral notes.
Mint cut in julienne releases more volatile aromatics; olive oil and lemon make a fresh dressing that balances the richness of the meat and purée.

creme-caramel.title: Crème caramel
creme-caramel.intro: Serves 4. A great French classic: a blond caramel at the bottom of each ramekin and a very smooth custard of milk, fleurette cream, sugar and eggs, baked gently in a bain-marie. Make ahead: chill several hours, ideally overnight.
steps: Caramel: pour 3 tablespoons water (45 g) over 120 g sugar (6 tablespoons) in a saucepan. Do not stir — if you stir, the sugar crystallises into a rocher. Heat to a blond amber, a little pushed: in the oven it loses some colour. Pour at once into 4 ramekins and tilt quickly to spread it. Let it harden a moment before pouring the custard.

Milk and cream: flatten a vanilla pod, split it along its full length, scrape the seeds. Warm 20 cl milk with 20 cl crème fleurette (pouring cream, about 30% fat), the seeds and the pod, to 65–70 °C, covered. Do not boil. Return the pod to the sugar.

Eggs: [blanchir the yolks](blanchir-les-jaunes) — pour 60 g sugar (3 tablespoons) all at once onto 2 whole eggs and 2 yolks. Whisk at once — sugar is a little acidic and will « cook » the yolks if it sits. Just enough to combine, without adding much air.
Temper: slowly pour the warm milk and cream into the eggs while mixing. Strain if possible. When the caramel has hardened in the ramekins, divide the custard over it.

Baking: place the ramekins in a baking dish, add hot water halfway up the sides. Bake at 150 °C for about 35 to 40 minutes, until the centre still jiggles slightly. Overbake and the custard tastes eggy.
Cooling and serving: cool, then chill for several hours. To unmould, run a thin blade around the edge and invert onto a plate so the caramel coats the custard.
chemistry: Caramel comes from the transformation of sugar under heat: it brings colour, gentle bitterness and toasted notes. One crystal, if you stir, seeds the whole recrystallisation — that is the rocher.

During gentle baking, egg proteins coagulate gradually and give the custard structure without making it grainy. Sugar left sitting on the yolks « cooks » them by osmosis: pour it all at once and whisk at once.
Fleurette cream, richer than milk, softens the egg flavour and makes a silkier texture; the bain-marie limits direct heat. Infusing the vanilla covered keeps the volatile aromas.

atelier.title: Workshop — 4 people, 4 ramekins
atelier.description: For a workshop with 4 participants, make one batter from the recipe for 4, then each person pours into her own ramekin. Count 20 cl milk, 20 cl crème fleurette, 2 whole eggs, 2 yolks, 60 g sugar for the custard and 120 g sugar for the caramel.
steps: Station 1 — Caramel: under supervision, pour 3 tablespoons water (45 g) over 120 g sugar. Do not stir. Push to a blond amber. Divide among the 4 ramekins, about 30 g sugar per ramekin. Let it harden.

Station 2 — Milk and cream: flatten, split and scrape a vanilla pod. Heat 20 cl milk with 20 cl crème fleurette, the seeds and the pod, to 65–70 °C, covered, without boiling. Return the pod to the sugar.
Station 3 — Eggs: pour 60 g sugar all at once onto 2 whole eggs and 2 yolks. Whisk at once, without making it too frothy.
Station 4 — Assembly: pour the hot liquid gradually into the eggs, strain, then fill the 4 ramekins once the caramel has hardened.

Shared baking: place the 4 ramekins in one dish, add hot water halfway up the sides and bake them all together in a bain-marie for 35 to 40 minutes at 150 °C, until the centre still jiggles. Cool, then chill.

dulce-de-leche.title: Dulce de leche
dulce-de-leche.intro: A basic preparation. Dulce de leche made by cooking a can of sweetened condensed milk in a bain-marie for 4 hours: the milk and sugar brown and thicken. A 397 g can yields about 350 g of dulce de leche, enough for the crêpes. Make ahead: cool completely before opening.
steps: Can: take one 397 g can of sweetened condensed milk, still sealed. Remove the label. Lay the can on its side in a large saucepan.
Water: cover with cold water, at least 3 to 4 cm above the can. Bring to a gentle simmer, never a hard boil.
Cooking: simmer gently for 4 hours. The water must never drop below the can: top up with hot water if needed.
Cooling: turn off the heat and leave the can to cool completely in the water, several hours, before opening. Never open it hot.
Result: an amber, thick, glossy dulce de leche. Stir to smooth if needed. Keep refrigerated in a closed jar.
chemistry: Long, moist heat makes the sugars in condensed milk (lactose and sucrose) react with the milk proteins: that is the [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard), which gives the amber colour and caramel taste.
Over 4 hours the proteins denature and the mixture thickens; the longer the cook, the darker and more intense the dulce.
The sealed can under water cooks without air: the dulce stays smooth, with no crust or drying out.

creme-brulee.title: Creme brulee
creme-brulee.intro: Serves 4. Traditional French creme brulee: a rich vanilla custard made with cream, sugar and egg yolks, finished with a thin layer of caramelised sugar just before serving.
steps: Ratios: count 10 cl heavy cream, 1 tablespoon sugar and 1 egg yolk per person. For 4 people, use 40 cl cream, 4 tablespoons sugar and 4 egg yolks.
Cream: warm the cream gently with 1 split vanilla pod or a little extract, without boiling.
Custard base: [blanchir the yolks](blanchir-les-jaunes) — whisk the yolks with the sugar just enough to combine, without adding too much air. Pour in the hot cream gradually while stirring.

Baking: divide into ramekins. Bain-marie: hot water halfway up the sides. Bake at 150 °C for about 35 to 40 minutes, until the centre still jiggles slightly. At 110 °C, count 1 hour 15 minutes. Overbake and the custard tastes eggy.
Cooling and finish: let cool completely, then chill. Just before serving, sprinkle on a thin layer of sugar and caramelise it with a blowtorch to form a thin, crisp crust.
chemistry: Egg yolks coagulate gently with heat and give creme brulee its smooth, silky texture.
Cream, which is richer in fat than milk, brings more richness and helps protect the custard texture from harsh heat.
The caramelised sugar layer contrasts with the cold custard underneath: that contrast between brittle top and creamy interior is what defines the dessert.

tournedos-boeuf-tian.title: Beef tournedos & provençal skewer
tournedos-boeuf-tian.intro: Serves 2. Two beef tournedos — heart of the fillet, 3–4 cm medallions. A pepper, butter and crème fraîche sauce, deglazed with red wine: it pools on the bottom of the plate. Beside it, a single [Provençal tian](tian-provencal) skewer — courgette, tomato, aubergine — roasted. Not the earthenware dish: one brochette per plate.
steps: Skewer: wash 1 courgette, 1 small aubergine, 2 firm tomatoes. Cut into rounds about 1 cm thick. Thread alternating — courgette, tomato, aubergine, as for the [tian](tian-provencal) — on 2 skewers. Olive oil, herbes de Provence, salt. One brochette per plate.
Oven: 200 °C. Roast the skewers 20 to 25 minutes, until the edges brown. Keep warm.
Tournedos: 2 beef fillet medallions (150–180 g, 3–4 cm). Pat dry. Take out 15–20 min. Salt. Crush black pepper in a mortar; crust both faces.
Sear: very hot pan, olive oil. Colour 2 to 3 minutes per side. Add a knob of [butter](beurre); baste. Lift out. Rest 3 minutes.
Deglaze: in the same pan, pour 8 cl red wine over the fond. Scrape. Reduce by half.
Sauce: off the heat, or over very low heat, beat in 30 g cold butter and 3 tablespoons [crème fraîche](creme). Whisk until it coats. Do not boil.
Plating: a pool of sauce on the bottom of the plate. Set the tournedos on it. The skewer beside, off the sauce.
chemistry: The crust of the tournedos: [Maillard reaction](reaction-maillard). The crushed pepper toasts a little; it seasons without turning to powder.
Red wine deglazes the fond: the juices dissolve, the alcohol leaves, the acidity stays.
Off the heat, butter and cream mount the wine: an emulsion, nappe. Too hot, the cream splits.
The skewer roasts apart: the same vegetables as the [tian](tian-provencal), dry heat, a single stick.

tournedos-rossini.title: Tournedos Rossini
tournedos-rossini.intro: A French classic: pan-seared beef tournedos topped with seared foie gras, served on a crouton with Madeira or port wine sauce and slices of truffle (optional but traditional).
steps: Take the meat and foie gras out of the fridge 20–30 minutes before cooking so they come to room temperature.
Make the sauce: sweat a finely chopped shallot in a little butter, deglaze with Madeira or port, reduce, add a little veal stock or meat jus, whisk in cold butter and keep warm.
Pan-fry the bread croutons in butter until golden on both sides; set aside.
In a very hot pan with a little neutral fat, sear the beef tournedos (3–4 cm thick) for 2–3 minutes per side for rare to medium-rare; salt at the end of cooking and rest for a few minutes under foil.
In a very hot pan (dry or with very little fat), quickly sear the foie gras escalopes (about 1.5–2 cm thick) for 1–2 minutes per side; season with salt and pepper.
To plate: place each tournedos on a crouton, top with a foie gras escalope, spoon over the Madeira sauce and, if you like, add a few slices of truffle.
chemistry: Resting the meat after cooking allows the juices to redistribute, giving a more tender, juicy texture.
The fat from the foie gras partially renders during cooking and flavours the meat and sauce, adding great richness.
Reducing the Madeira concentrates its sugars and aromas, giving a syrupy, intense sauce.
